value.overview: The Long-tailed Tyrant (Colonia colonus) is a distinctive small flycatcher named for the two greatly elongated central tail feathers, especially prominent in males. It is the only species in its genus and belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family. The species uses forest edges, clearings, river margins, and other partly open situations where it can make aerial sallies after insects. In Costa Rica it is known locally as the Mosquero coludo and is a resident of mainly lowland Caribbean habitats.
value.classification: The Long-tailed Tyrant is a passerine in the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. It is the sole species in the genus Colonia; the scientific name is Colonia colonus.
value.identification: This slim flycatcher has a short, relatively broad bill, an upright posture, and strikingly long central tail feathers. Adults are mostly dark gray to black, with contrasting white on the crown or forehead and on parts of the wings; the exact pattern varies with sex and subspecies. Females and immature birds can appear duller or browner than adult males. It often perches conspicuously on an exposed branch or snag, repeatedly flicking its tail and launching short flights after insects.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad but discontinuous distribution from southern Central America through much of northern, western, and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, chiefly of the Caribbean lowlands and foothills, generally below about 600 meters, with occasional records higher on slopes. It occupies humid evergreen forest edges, riverine woodland, plantations, second-growth areas, forest openings, and clearings containing standing trees or snags. It is often found in semi-open landscapes rather than deep, closed-canopy forest.
value.migrationStatus: Long-tailed Tyrants are generally resident throughout their range, including Costa Rica. Costa Rican birds are not considered regular long-distance migrants, although local movements may occur, and populations at the southern edge of the range may shift seasonally.
value.breeding: The Long-tailed Tyrant nests in natural cavities, abandoned woodpecker holes, or similar openings in trees, usually in forest-edge or semi-open habitat. The nest is placed above the ground and may be associated with a snag or living tree. Available accounts indicate that the species lays a small clutch, commonly about two eggs. Both adults are involved in territorial defense and care of the young, but detailed breeding information is limited in some parts of its range, including Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on flying insects, including bees and other small insects. In Costa Rica, stingless bees may form an important part of its diet. The bird usually hunts from a conspicuous perch, making quick aerial sallies to capture prey and often returning to the same branch. It may forage alone, in pairs, or in small family groups, and it is not typically associated with mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: The species is active and conspicuous, often sitting upright on an exposed branch with its long tail hanging below the perch. Tail flicking and short, repeated flights are characteristic. It commonly defends a feeding or breeding area and may use the same favored perches repeatedly. Long-tailed Tyrants are usually encountered singly or in pairs, although family groups can occur after breeding. Their open perches and aerial hunting style make them easier to detect than many forest flycatchers.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not reliably established in the available assessment information.
